newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-US wheat sowings plunge, grain stocks shrink.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-US wheat sowings plunge, grain stocks shrink.

text.p: U.S. farmers sowed only 48.2 million acres of winter wheat -- a seven-percent decline that hinted at tight supplies for a year to come -- and other Agriculture Department reports Friday said the corn and soybean stockpiles would quickly dwindle to scanty levels.

Futures prices soared on the Chicago Board of Trade following release of the bundle of reports. Corn and soybeans hit the daily limit immediately afterwards, but retreated slightly from those highs later. Wheat was up as much as 11 cents a bushel at midday.
"The biggest shocker...was the winter wheat acreage number, the lowest since 1978," Dan Basse of the Chicago-based analytical firm AgResource Co. told reporters.

Grain and soybean prices have gyrated for the past two years because of short U.S. supplies, but food prices have been fairly stable. Even though U.S. farmers grew the third-largest corn crop and the second-largest soybean crop on record in 1996, it was barely ahead of voracious demand.

The 48.2 million acres of winter wheat provided the first look at possible crop output for the new year. Analysts had expected 51.4 million acres would be planted to winter wheat, just down from 52 million planted for last year's crop.
Private analyst John Schnittker said the lower acreage could reduce U.S. wheat output by 120 million bushels.

Winter wheat, which is planted in the fall and harvested the following summer, is the major U.S. wheat crop. Small acreage could lead to a small U.S. wheat harvest unless yields climbed or spring wheat acreage expanded.

An Agriculture Department official said spring wheat acreage often rebounded when winter wheat acreage slumped but another was less willing to speculate, saying the new "Freedom to Farm" law has given wheat farmers some incentive to plant other crops.

The Agriculture Department forecast U.S. stockpiles would shrink to 374 million bushels of wheat, 155 million bushels of soybeans and 959 million bushels of corn before the new crops were mature. The corn and soybean estimates were between one and two percent smaller than a month ago.

Mike Hoover of analysts WEFA Group in suburban Philadelphia said smaller stockpiles would undergird prices. WEFA anticipates farmers will plant about 80 million acres of corn and 64 million acres or so of soybeans.
"We expect to see a significant amount of corn planted as well as soybeans," Hoover said. "That should add some downward pressure on prices this fall."

Some 1.82 billion bushels of soybeans and 6.91 billion bushels of corn were in U.S. bins and warehouses on December 1, forming the U.S. supply for the next several months. The "stocks" figures were slightly smaller than analysts expected, which helped propel prices higher on futures markets.

In its final look at 1996 crop output, the department slightly raised its corn estimate to 9.29 billion bushels, marginally reduced soybeans to 2.382 billion bushels and held wheat at 2.281 billion bushels.
